A.explanation: Starts at zero velocity at $t=0$, becomes maximum upward when displacement is zero, and zero at maximum upward displacement, matching the gradient of the displacement graph.

B.explanation: Starts at maximum upward velocity, which would mean the mass is passing equilibrium at $t=0$, but it is released from rest at maximum distance down.

C.explanation: Shows twice the frequency of the displacement oscillation, but velocity in simple oscillation has the same period as displacement.

D.explanation: Shows velocity never negative, but the mass must move down with negative velocity for half of each oscillation.

hints: Notice the displacement graph starts at maximum distance down at $t=0$ with zero gradient, so the initial velocity must be zero.
Recall velocity is the gradient of displacement with upward as positive, so velocity is positive while the displacement curve slopes upward.
Connect maximum speed to the times the displacement crosses zero and zero speed to the times of maximum up or down displacement.
walkthrough: At $t=0$ the mass is released from maximum distance down, so displacement is most negative and the curve is flat. Gradient is zero, so velocity up is $0$.
Just after $t=0$ the displacement curve slopes upward toward equilibrium, so the gradient and hence velocity up are positive and increasing.

Velocity up is maximum where the displacement gradient is steepest, which is at the first zero crossing of displacement. It then falls to zero at the peak distance up where the displacement gradient is again zero.
After the peak the mass moves down, so the displacement gradient and velocity up become negative, reaching most negative at the next zero crossing, then returning to zero.
This gives a sine-like velocity curve starting at $0$, going positive first, with the same period as displacement. This is option A.
